note: _neminem per viam salutaveritis_ – and salute no man by the way (Douay Version); you are to give no one greeting on your way (Knox). Possibly, _salutare_ means here more than mere greeting; it may actually mean “to visit,” which may be the implication of the injunction, see Bernhard Lang: Grußverbot oder Besuchsverbot? Eine sozialgeschichtliche Deutung von Lukas 10,4b. _Biblische Zeitschrift_ 26 (1982) 75–79.

_duxit in stabulum_ – he brought him to an inn (Douay Version). The noun _stabulum_ is rendered “tavern” by Richards (p. 115). Meant is no doubt a simple place for staying over night, because elsewhere (2 Chr 9:25), the word is used for putting up animals (like “stable” in English). – (Joseph) Heinrich Vogels: Stabulum. _Biblische Zeitschrift_ 11 (1913) 4.

_quis videtur tibi proximus fuisse illi_. In the Latin, the question about the neighbor is misleading; it should be: _proximum egisse_ (the question is: who behaved as a neighbour?). Many modern translations – including the Bible de Jérusalem – translate correctly. The neighbor is the poor man, not the Samaritan. – Guillaume Cardascia: Sur quelques erreurs de la Vulgate. Nombres 5,31 – Luc 10,36. _Revue biblique_ 111 (2004) 419–422.
